Once you're experiencing it, you can grow so much from it. Once you experience it, you can go further, much further. It's a feeling of it. We were quite poor, we had no money, my parents were working really hard. When I grew up, I saw them working so hard, and then deep inside myself that I wanted to change the situation, I wanted to make something, this one thing. Stevens: What do you think are the most important qualities for a businessperson? Tam: For me, it's most important, a vision, determination, and to never say no to yourself. Stevens: You work in a very creative industry, how do you keep your staff motivated in this industry, how do you keep them going, how do you keep them working for you? Tam: I always tell them my story, how I was in school when my teacher asked for one outfit -- I give them 8 outfits. I told them, do things that I didn't ask you, give me, do your work with passion, it's more important than "Oh, 6 o'clock, I have to leave." Do something that is out of the box. E-mail to a friend .

**HONG KONG, China (CNN)** -- From the runway to the store rack, Vivienne Tam stands out as a designer who balances creativity and business acumen in equal measure. The leading fashion designer spoke to CNN's Andrew Stevens in The Boardroom.

Since launching her career in the fashion industry in the early '80s and establishing her own brand in the '90s, Tam has risen to prominence with her distinctive east-meets-west aesthetic. Today, it is her business expertise that has expanded the label to some 30 stores worldwide, from New York to Beijing. CNN's Andrew Stevens caught up with the designer in Hong Kong to discuss what it takes to lead both the commercial and creative direction of a global fashion line.

**Tam:** The business side is much like designing. Just as I love the feel of a fabric and the desire to understand its details, I feel my way through a deal and take the time to know it thoroughly—because who better understands the best deal for you than yourself? It's just like designing clothes; I love to know how to solve every single thing, right down to what kind of budget is required.

**Stevens:** Is it simply natural curiosity?

**Tam:** Natural curiosity—I love it. I love every aspect of it.

**Stevens:** Who did you learn your business skills from, or did you make it up as you went along?

**Tam:** I taught myself everything about business. I knew nothing at the start, and I learned it all—the pricing, the shipping, the contracts, everything—simply by doing it. When you do it yourself, you truly understand everything. If you don't, and you merely listen to someone else explain how it's done, you never experience it firsthand. Once you experience it, you grow immensely. Once you experience it, you can go much, much further. It's a matter of feeling it.

**Stevens:** When you won the Hong Kong Businesswoman of the Year award, you said your mother was one of your greatest inspirations. How did she inspire you?

**Tam:** She inspired me tremendously—with, as you say, her determination and persistence. When she truly set her mind on something, she would see it through to the very end; she was determined to make it happen. I see her as the driving force behind me. We were quite poor and had no money, and my parents worked incredibly hard. Growing up, I watched them labor so tirelessly, and deep within me a desire took root—I wanted to change our situation, I wanted to achieve something, this one thing.

**Stevens:** What do you believe are the most important qualities for a businessperson?

**Tam:** For me, the most important are vision, determination, and never saying no to yourself. You must also remain open—open to learning, open to criticism, and open to the fact that you know nothing about the business. By knowing nothing, you can learn everything and succeed in areas you never imagined.

**Stevens:** You work in a highly creative industry. How do you keep your staff motivated, how do you keep them going, and how do you keep them working for you?

**Tam:** I always share my own story with them—how, back in school, when my teacher asked for a single outfit, I would present eight. I tell them to do more than what I ask, to bring passion to their work, because that matters far more than watching the clock and thinking, "Oh, it's six o'clock, I have to leave." Do something that is out of the box.

*E-mail to a friend*

HONG KONG, China (CNN) -- Vivienne Tam stands out as a designer who blends artistic vision with sharp commercial instincts, guiding her work all the way from the catwalk to retail shelves. The prominent fashion designer sat down with CNN's Andrew Stevens in The Boardroom. After entering the fashion world in the early 1980s and launching her personal label in the 1990s, she gained recognition for her distinctive fusion of eastern and western aesthetics. These days, her business talents have grown the brand into roughly 30 outlets across the globe, stretching from New York all the way to Beijing. CNN's Andrew Stevens met with her in Hong Kong to explore what it means to steer both the commercial and artistic sides of an international fashion brand.

Tam: Handling the business feels similar to designing to me -- just as I enjoy the texture of fabric and want to understand its details, I want to grasp the specifics of a deal. You develop a sense for it and understand it, because really, who else knows what deal suits you best? Only you do. It parallels creating clothing; I want to figure out how to work through every issue, right down to things like budgeting.

Stevens: So it's simply natural curiosity?

Tam: Yes, natural curiosity -- I adore it. I enjoy every part of the process.

Stevens: Did someone teach you your business abilities, or did you figure it out as you went?

Tam: I taught myself everything about business. I started out knowing nothing, and I picked up all of it -- pricing, shipping, contracts, all of it -- by actually doing the work. Handling things personally is how you truly understand them. If you never do it yourself and only hear someone else explain the process, you're not really living it. But once you've been through it firsthand, you can grow tremendously. That experience lets you advance much further. It comes down to a feeling for it.

Stevens: When you were named Hong Kong's businesswoman of the year, you mentioned that your mother was among your biggest inspirations. In what way did she inspire you?

Tam: She was a huge inspiration to me -- exactly like you mentioned, that determination and persistence. Whenever she set her mind on accomplishing something, she'd see it through completely; she was absolutely committed to making it happen. Looking at her, I realized she's truly the driving force behind me. We didn't have much -- we were quite poor and my parents labored intensely. Growing up watching them work so hard, I felt a deep desire within me to change our circumstances, to create something meaningful.

Stevens: In your view, what are the essential traits for someone in business?

Tam: For me, the crucial ones are having a vision, staying determined, and never telling yourself no. You also have to stay receptive to criticism and open to learning. Being willing to admit you know nothing about business actually lets you learn everything from that blank slate, and then succeed at things you never previously understood.

Stevens: Your field is highly creative -- how do you keep your team inspired, driven, and dedicated to working for you?

Tam: I always share my own story with them -- how back in school, when a teacher requested a single outfit, I would produce eight instead. I encourage them to go beyond what I've asked, to bring passion to their work, which matters far more than watching the clock and thinking, "It's 6 o'clock, time to go." I want them to create something outside the box.

Vivienne Tam stands as a remarkable example of a designer who combines creativity and business acumen in equal measure. Since rising to fame in the early 1980s, she has captivated the fashion world with her distinctive east-meets-west styles, seamlessly blending elements of her cultural heritage with contemporary Western sensibilities to create a truly unique aesthetic.

Fashion designer Vivienne Tam has spent decades cultivating a brand that seamlessly blends Eastern heritage with Western sensibilities. What began as a singular creative vision has grown into a global enterprise with roughly 30 stores around the world. # Hong Kong: A Vibrant Fusion of East and West

Hong Kong stands as one of the world's most dynamic and captivating destinations, a Special Administrative Region of China that seamlessly blends Eastern traditions with Western influences. Located on the southeastern coast of China, this bustling metropolis has earned its reputation as a global financial hub and a gateway between mainland China and the rest of the world.

## A Brief History

Hong Kong was a British colony for over 150 years before its handover to China in 1997. Under the "One Country, Two Systems" principle, Hong Kong maintains a high degree of autonomy, preserving its own legal system, economic policies, and way of life while remaining part of China. This unique arrangement has shaped the city's distinctive character and identity.

## Economic Powerhouse

As one of the world's leading international financial centers, Hong Kong plays a crucial role in China's economy. The city serves as a vital link for international trade and investment flowing in and out of mainland China. Its free-market economy, low taxation, and robust legal framework have attracted businesses from around the globe, making it a preferred destination for multinational corporations establishing their Asian headquarters.

## Cultural Melting Pot

Hong Kong's culture reflects its rich heritage as a meeting point of civilizations. Traditional Chinese customs coexist with modern cosmopolitan lifestyles. Visitors can explore ancient temples nestled between towering skyscrapers, experience vibrant street markets, and savor world-renowned Cantonese cuisine alongside international dining options.

## A City of Contrasts

The stunning skyline of Hong Kong, particularly around Victoria Harbour, is among the most photographed in the world. Yet beyond the urban landscape, the region offers surprising natural beauty, including lush country parks, pristine beaches, and mountainous hiking trails.

## Conclusion

Hong Kong remains an extraordinary place where China's ancient traditions meet contemporary global culture. Its resilience, energy, and unique position continue to make it a fascinating and important city on the world stage.

# From Silk Roads to Silicon Valley: Vivienne Tam on Fashion, Business, and Bridging Cultures

*In a career spanning more than three decades, designer Vivienne Tam has built a global brand by blending East and West—turning cultural heritage into commercial success. CNN sat down with the celebrated designer to discuss her journey, her business philosophy, and how she stays relevant in a fast-changing industry.*

---

**CNN: You were born in Guangzhou, China, and raised in Hong Kong before making your name in New York. How did that multicultural background shape your design sensibility?**

**Vivienne Tam:** Growing up between two worlds gave me a unique lens. In Hong Kong, I was surrounded by traditional Chinese culture, but I was also exposed to Western influences everywhere—in music, film, and fashion. I never saw East and West as opposites. To me, they were meant to blend together. That fusion became the DNA of my brand. When I moved to New York in the 1980s, I wanted to tell stories about my heritage in a way that felt modern and universal.

---

**CNN: Your "Mao Collection" in 1995 became iconic. What was the thinking behind such a bold, provocative statement?**

**Vivienne Tam:** That collection came from a place of playfulness and cultural commentary. I took the image of Chairman Mao and reimagined it—Mao with bees on his nose, Mao in pop-art colors. It was about taking something politically heavy and giving it lightness, humor, and art. It caused a sensation. Some pieces are now in the Victoria and Albert Museum and the Andy Warhol Museum. For me, it proved that fashion can be a canvas for ideas, not just clothing.

---

**CNN: Let's talk business. Fashion is notoriously difficult to sustain financially. What has been your secret to longevity?**

**Vivienne Tam:** You have to be both creative *and* disciplined. A lot of designers focus only on the art and forget the business. I learned early that you need to understand your customer, manage your production costs, and build relationships with retailers. I studied the numbers as much as I studied the fabrics. Diversifying was also key—I moved beyond apparel into accessories, fragrance, home goods, and technology. Never rely on a single revenue stream.

---

**CNN: You made headlines by partnering with Hewlett-Packard to design laptops. That was ahead of its time. What inspired that move?**

**Vivienne Tam:** I saw technology becoming a part of everyday fashion long before others did. Why should a laptop be a boring gray box? I wanted to bring beauty and personal expression to gadgets. The HP collaboration in 2008 created what many called the world's first "digital clutch." It sold out quickly and opened a whole new market. That taught me an important lesson: innovation means going where your industry hasn't gone yet.

---

**CNN: How do you approach the balance between staying true to your artistic vision and meeting market demands?**

**Vivienne Tam:** It's a constant conversation. I never compromise my core identity—my aesthetic has to be authentic. But I also listen carefully to the market. Fashion is a dialogue with your customers. You give them your vision, and they tell you what resonates. The designers who fail are the ones who either ignore the market completely or chase trends and lose themselves. The goal is to evolve without losing your soul.

---

**CNN: What role has China's growth played in your business strategy?**

**Vivienne Tam:** Enormous. As China's economy grew, so did a new generation of consumers who wanted brands that honored their heritage while feeling international. I was well-positioned because that's exactly what I've always done. I've expanded significantly across Asia, opening boutiques and forming partnerships. Understanding both the Western and Chinese markets has been my competitive advantage. I can be a bridge between the two.

---

**CNN: You've weathered economic downturns, the rise of fast fashion, and now the digital revolution. How do you adapt?**

**Vivienne Tam:** By staying curious and never being afraid to reinvent. When e-commerce took off, I embraced it. When social media changed how brands connect with people, I leaned in. I think the biggest mistake in business is complacency. The moment you think you've "made it," you become vulnerable. I approach every season as if I'm proving myself again.

---

**CNN: What advice would you give to young designers who want to build not just a label, but a sustainable business?**

**Vivienne Tam:** First, know who you are—your voice is your greatest asset. Second, learn the business side, even if it doesn't excite you. Understand contracts, margins, and marketing. Third, build a strong team; you can't do everything alone. And finally, be patient. Overnight success is a myth. My career was built one relationship, one collection, one lesson at a time.

---

**CNN: Looking back, what are you most proud of?**

**Vivienne Tam:** That I've stayed true to my story while building something that lasts. I've shown that you can honor your culture and still succeed on a global stage. Fashion, for me, has always been about connection—connecting people, cultures, and ideas. If my work has inspired others to embrace their own heritage with pride, that's my greatest achievement.

---

*Vivienne Tam continues to design from her New York studio while expanding her presence across Asia. Her memoir, "China Chic," remains a celebrated exploration of Chinese aesthetics and their influence on modern design.*

# CNN Business Feature: The Art of Fashion

## Andrew Stevens Interviews Designer Vivienne Tam

*[TRANSCRIPT]*

---

**ANDREW STEVENS:** Welcome back to CNN. I'm Andrew Stevens, coming to you from Hong Kong, a city that bridges East and West—much like my guest today. Vivienne Tam has built a global fashion brand rooted in her Chinese heritage while conquering the runways of New York. Vivienne, thank you for joining us.

**VIVIENNE TAM:** Thank you, Andrew. It's wonderful to be here, especially in Hong Kong. This city means so much to me.

**STEVENS:** Let's start there. You grew up here in Hong Kong before moving to New York. How has this city shaped your creative vision?

**TAM:** Hong Kong is where East meets West—that fusion is in my blood. You see the traditional and the modern side by side, the temples next to skyscrapers. That contrast, that harmony, it's the foundation of everything I create. My designs are about telling that story of cultural connection.

**STEVENS:** Speaking of storytelling—your famous "Mao" collection back in the '90s really put you on the map. But fashion is also a business. How do you balance artistic expression with commercial reality?

**TAM:** That's the eternal question, isn't it? For me, creativity always comes first—but creativity without sustainability is just a hobby. You have to understand your customer. I never design something purely for the runway spectacle. I ask, "Will a woman feel beautiful and confident wearing this? Will it fit her life?"

**STEVENS:** So you're thinking about the wearer, not just the art?

**TAM:** Exactly. Art and commerce aren't enemies. The most successful designs are the ones that touch people emotionally *and* make sense in the market. When I did my collaboration with HP on laptops, people said, "Fashion and technology?" But I saw an opportunity to bring beauty into everyday objects. That's business *and* creativity together.

**STEVENS:** Let's talk about that. You were early to embrace technology partnerships. Was that a calculated business decision or an artistic instinct?

**TAM:** *[laughs]* Both! I trust my instincts, but I also watch where the world is going. Technology is part of our lives now. If fashion ignores that, it becomes irrelevant. I wanted to democratize design—make beautiful things accessible. That's good business and good philosophy.

**STEVENS:** The fashion industry has faced real disruption—fast fashion, e-commerce, changing consumer habits. How do you stay relevant?

**TAM:** You have to evolve without losing your soul. My aesthetic—that East-meets-West sensibility—that never changes. It's my signature. But *how* I reach people, how I sell, how I market? That must constantly adapt. Social media, online retail—these are tools. I embrace them, but I don't let them dictate my identity.

**STEVENS:** A lot of young designers watching this dream of building their own brand. What's the hardest business lesson you've learned?

**TAM:** *[pauses]* That talent alone is not enough. When I was young, I thought if the designs were beautiful, success would follow. But you must understand production, cash flow, relationships, timing. You need a strong team. I've learned to surround myself with people who understand the numbers so I can focus on the vision—but I still stay informed. Never hand over your business completely.

**STEVENS:** That's powerful advice. And China's market—how important is it to your growth strategy?

**TAM:** Enormously. The Chinese consumer is sophisticated, proud of their heritage, and hungry for design that reflects their identity with a global sensibility. That's exactly what I offer. For me, returning to China isn't just business—it's coming home. But yes, the opportunity is tremendous.

**STEVENS:** Before we go—after decades in this industry, what keeps you passionate?

**TAM:** The creating. Every collection is a new story, a new discovery. When I see a woman wearing my design and she feels empowered, feels beautiful—that's everything. The business allows me to keep creating. That's the balance. One serves the other.

**STEVENS:** Vivienne Tam, a masterclass in blending art and enterprise. Thank you so much.

**TAM:** Thank you, Andrew. It's been a pleasure.

**STEVENS:** For CNN, I'm Andrew Stevens in Hong Kong.

---

*[END TRANSCRIPT]*

# Bridging Worlds: A Conversation with Mei-Lin Chen

*The visionary behind LOTUS & LINEN talks self-education, maternal wisdom, and building a team that believes*

---

There's a particular energy in Mei-Lin Chen's studio—part Shanghai atelier, part Milanese design house. Bolts of silk brocade lean against industrial steel shelving. A vintage sewing machine that belonged to her grandmother sits beneath a wall of mood boards. When she greets me, it's with a firm handshake and an unhurried warmth.

At 44, Chen has built LOTUS & LINEN into a globally recognized label celebrated for its fusion of Eastern craftsmanship and Western silhouettes. But her path here was anything but conventional.

---

**You studied fine art, not business or fashion. How did you learn to run a company?**

I learned the way most people learn to swim when someone tosses them in the water. [*laughs*] When I started, I had exactly one thing: a point of view. I knew what I wanted the clothes to *say*. I knew nothing about margins, or supply chains, or how to read a balance sheet.

So I read everything. I bought secondhand business textbooks. I asked shop owners in my neighborhood how they handled inventory. I made every mistake you can make—I once ordered fabric for a full collection before I had a single confirmed buyer. That taught me more than any MBA could.

**Was there a turning point?**

The moment I stopped being embarrassed about what I didn't know. Early on, I'd nod along in meetings pretending to understand terms I didn't. One day a supplier used a word I didn't recognize, and instead of nodding, I just said, "I don't know what that means. Explain it to me." He did. And I realized the people who ask the questions are the ones who eventually run the room.

---

**Your mother comes up often in interviews. Tell me about her influence.**

My mother was a seamstress. Not a designer—a seamstress. She altered other people's clothes for money we badly needed. I used to sit on the floor of her workroom watching her hands.

What she gave me wasn't a love of fashion, exactly. It was a respect for *making*. She used to say, "The inside of a garment matters even when no one sees it." She meant the seams, the finishing—but I've come to understand she meant something larger. Do the work properly when no one is watching. That's the whole philosophy of my company, honestly.

**Did she live to see your success?**

She saw the beginning of it. She got to walk into my first real boutique. She didn't say much—she wasn't a woman of many words—but she ran her fingers along the hem of one of the dresses, checking the stitching. And then she nodded. That nod meant more to me than any review I've ever received.

---

**Your brand is built on "east meets west." Is that a personal identity or a business strategy?**

It's not a strategy at all—that would make it hollow. It's simply who I am. I grew up between two cultures, never fully belonging to either. For a long time that felt like a wound. The clothes were how I turned it into a language.

The mistake people make is treating "fusion" as decoration—slap a mandarin collar on a blazer and call it a day. Real fusion is about *tension*. Structure and flow. Restraint and expression. I want a woman to feel both grounded and free when she wears my work.

---

**Let's talk about your staff. You have a reputation for extraordinary loyalty—people stay with you for years. How do you motivate a team?**

I don't believe in motivating people. I believe in *not demotivating* them. Most talented people already arrive motivated. Your job as a leader is to remove the things that crush that.

So I'm ruthless about clarity. Nothing kills a person's spirit faster than working hard on the wrong thing. I make sure everyone knows not just *what* we're doing, but *why*.

**And beyond clarity?**

Credit. I give it away constantly and publicly. When a collection succeeds, I make sure the room knows exactly whose hands built it. Insecure leaders hoard credit. It's the cheapest resource you have and the most powerful.

I also share my own failures openly. If my team sees me admit I misjudged a launch, they stop fearing their own mistakes. And a team that isn't afraid will take the creative risks that actually move you forward.

**Do you see any of your mother in the way you lead?**

Every day. She never raised her voice, but people worked hard for her because she noticed things. She'd remember that a client's daughter was sick, or that an assistant had mentioned a birthday. Attention is a form of respect. I try to give my people that same attention—not as a management tactic, but because they deserve it.

---

**Final question. What would you tell a young designer standing where you stood twenty years ago?**

Two things. First—your outsider status is not your weakness, it's your material. Whatever makes you feel like you don't fit, that's the thing only you can offer.

Second—learn the business. Don't romanticize being "just a creative." The designers who control their vision are the ones who understand the numbers underneath it. Art and commerce aren't enemies. Handled well, they hold each other up. Rather like a good seam.

*She smiles, and for a moment glances at her grandmother's sewing machine in the corner.*

The inside matters, even when no one sees it.

---

*LOTUS & LINEN's new collection launches this spring.*

# THE BOARDROOM

## Where Creativity Meets Commerce: The Designer Who Refuses to Choose

*In our ongoing series profiling the leaders reshaping global business, CNN examines the rare executive who commands both the runway and the balance sheet.*

---

By the time most fashion houses have finished their morning coffee, Mei-Lin Zhao has already reviewed overnight sales figures from three continents, approved a fabric sourcing contract, and sketched the opening look for next season's collection.

"People assume you have to pick a side," Zhao says, seated in the minimalist glass-walled headquarters of AURELIA, the brand she founded fourteen years ago. "The artist or the CEO. The dreamer or the operator. I never accepted that this was a real choice."

That refusal has built something remarkable: a fashion house now valued at an estimated $1.2 billion, with 340 retail locations spanning Singapore, Shanghai, London, New York, and eleven other markets—all while Zhao retains majority creative and operational control.

### From Workshop to Global Brand

Zhao's origin story has become industry legend. Raised above her family's tailoring shop in Kuala Lumpur, she learned pattern-cutting before she learned algebra.

"My mother could look at a customer and know their measurements without a tape," Zhao recalls. "That was my first lesson in understanding the person, not just the garment. Every business decision I make still starts with that question: who is this actually for?"

After studying design in London and spending a formative three years on the finance side of a European luxury conglomerate—an unusual detour for a creative—Zhao returned to Asia in 2010 to launch AURELIA with a modest investment and what she calls "an unreasonable amount of conviction."

### The Dual-Track Philosophy

What distinguishes Zhao from her peers isn't merely that she oversees both design and business—it's her insistence that the two functions inform each other constantly.

"The wall companies build between the studio and the boardroom is expensive," she explains. "When designers don't understand margins, they create beautiful things nobody can afford to produce. When executives don't understand craft, they cut the details that made the brand worth buying."

Her solution has been structural. AURELIA holds joint "creative-commercial reviews" where designers sit alongside supply-chain analysts. Merchandisers attend fabric development meetings. It's a system Zhao admits took years to refine.

"The first attempts were chaos," she laughs. "Two languages, two egos. But eventually people started speaking each other's grammar."

### Betting on Sustainability Before It Sold

In 2016, Zhao made a decision that alarmed her investors: committing to fully traceable supply chains and recycled materials across the entire product line, absorbing significant short-term costs.

"The board was nervous. Frankly, I was nervous," she admits. "But I could see where the customer was moving. Leadership sometimes means being early enough to look wrong."

The gamble paid off. AURELIA's transparency reporting is now cited as an industry benchmark, and the sustainability line accounts for nearly 40% of revenue.

### The Weight of Both Crowns

Wearing two hats carries a cost. Zhao is candid about the exhaustion of context-switching between a color palette and a P&L statement within the same hour.

"There are days the CEO in me and the designer in me argue all the way home," she says. "The designer wants to chase beauty without limits. The CEO reminds her that a brand that doesn't survive can't create anything."

She's also thinking about legacy and succession—an issue that has quietly ended many founder-led fashion empires.

"I'm building a company that doesn't depend entirely on me," she says. "That's harder than it sounds when your name is stitched into the identity. But a leader's real product is the organization that outlasts them."

### The Boardroom Takeaway

Asked what she'd tell young leaders trying to bridge the creative-commercial divide, Zhao doesn't hesitate.

"Stop apologizing for caring about both. The market rewards clarity, but it rewards vision too. The future belongs to the people brave enough to hold both in their hands—and steady enough not to drop either."

As our interview ends, an assistant delivers a stack of fabric swatches and a quarterly forecast to the same desk. Zhao reaches for both.

---

*THE BOARDROOM airs weekly, spotlighting the executives redefining global leadership.*

---

**Note:** This is a fictional profile created for illustrative purposes in the style of a CNN business segment. Mei-Lin Zhao and AURELIA are invented for this article and do not represent real individuals or companies.

# From Passion to Prosperity: A Conversation with a Self-Made Fashion Visionary

*In an industry often dominated by prestigious design school pedigrees, one entrepreneur has carved her own path through sheer determination and hands-on learning. We sat down to discuss her journey, her philosophy, and her advice for the next generation of dreamers.*

---

When you walk into her studio, you immediately sense that this is a space built by hands that have known both struggle and triumph. Fabric swatches line the walls, sketches cover every surface, and there's an energy that speaks to years of relentless work. Yet the woman at the center of it all is remarkably grounded.

"I never went to design school," she tells me with a smile that suggests she's proud of this fact rather than apologetic. "Everything I know, I learned by doing—by failing, by trying again, and by refusing to give up."

## The Early Days

Her story begins, as many great stories do, with limited resources and boundless ambition.

"I started with a secondhand sewing machine and about fifty dollars in savings," she recalls. "I didn't have connections. I didn't have a business degree. What I had was a vision and the stubbornness to pursue it."

Those early years were far from glamorous. She describes long nights teaching herself pattern-making from library books, watching tutorials, and reverse-engineering garments she admired.

"I would take apart clothes just to understand how they were constructed," she says. "Every mistake taught me something. There's no textbook that can replace the education you get from actually making things wrong a hundred times before you get them right."

## On Determination

When I ask what quality has been most essential to her success, she doesn't hesitate.

"Determination. Without question. Talent is everywhere—the world is full of talented people who gave up. What separates the successful ones is the willingness to keep going when everything tells you to stop."

She leans forward, her expression intensifying.

"There were moments I wanted to quit. Orders fell through. Suppliers let me down. I had seasons where I barely broke even. But I made a decision early on: I would treat every setback as information, not as a verdict on my worth."

This mindset, she believes, is teachable—though it requires effort.

"People think determination is something you either have or you don't. I disagree. You build it. Every time you push through a hard moment, you're strengthening that muscle. It gets easier to trust yourself."

## Learning by Doing

Her philosophy on education is refreshingly practical, and she's passionate about the value of hands-on experience.

"I respect formal education, truly. But I want young people to know that it's not the only route. Some of the best lessons can't be taught in a classroom—they have to be lived."

She points to a mannequin draped in one of her signature pieces.

"That design came from a failure. An entire collection I thought was going to launch my career flopped. But in the wreckage of that flop, I discovered a technique that became my whole aesthetic. If I'd been too afraid to experiment, I would never have found it."

For her, the fear of failure is the real enemy.

"Learning by doing means you have to be comfortable being bad at something before you're good at it. Most people can't tolerate that discomfort. But that discomfort is exactly where growth lives."

## The Business Behind the Beauty

Fashion may be an art, but she's quick to remind me that it's also a business—and one she had to learn from scratch.

"The creative side came naturally to me. The business side did not," she admits with a laugh. "I had to teach myself accounting, marketing, negotiation, everything. I made expensive mistakes. But I refused to be one of those artists who dismisses the business as beneath them. If you want your art to reach people, you have to understand commerce."

She credits her willingness to wear multiple hats for her longevity.

"For years, I was the designer, the seamstress, the accountant, the shipping department, and the customer service team all at once. It was exhausting, but I learned every part of my company from the inside out. Now, when I hire people, I understand exactly what their jobs require."

## Qualities for Success

I ask her to name the qualities she believes are essential for anyone hoping to build something of their own. She counts them off thoughtfully.

**Resilience.** "You will be knocked down. Repeatedly. Success belongs to the people who get back up one more time than they fall."

**Curiosity.** "Stay a student forever. The moment you think you know everything, you stop growing. I'm still learning new things every single day."

**Discipline.** "Passion gets you started, but discipline keeps you going. Inspiration is unreliable. Showing up every day, whether you feel like it or not—that's what builds a career."

**Authenticity.** "Don't try to be someone else. The market doesn't need another copy. It needs your unique voice. My biggest breakthroughs came when I stopped imitating others and started trusting my own perspective."

**Adaptability.** "The world changes fast, especially in fashion. What worked yesterday won't work tomorrow. You have to be willing to evolve without losing your core."

## Advice for the Next Generation

As our conversation draws to a close, I ask what she would say to a young woman sitting where she once sat—with a dream, a modest budget, and no clear roadmap.

She pauses, choosing her words carefully.

"I'd tell her that not knowing how to do something isn't a reason to stop. It's an invitation to learn. Every expert was once a beginner who refused to quit."

"I'd tell her that the path won't be linear, and that's okay. The detours often teach you more than the straight roads ever could."

"And I'd tell her this: believe in your vision even when no one else does. Especially then. Because if you don't bet on yourself, why should anyone else?"

She glances around her studio—the physical manifestation of decades of that self-belief.

"I built all of this without permission from anyone. That's not arrogance. It's the simple truth that you don't need someone else to validate your dream before you begin. You just have to start, and you have to keep going."

---

*As I leave her studio, I'm struck by the realization that her success was never really about fashion at all. It was about a way of moving through the world—with grit, with curiosity, and with an unshakeable belief in the power of showing up, day after day, to build the life you envision. In a culture obsessed with overnight success, her story is a powerful reminder that the most enduring achievements are usually the ones we build with our own two hands.*
